segments.say: Of all the things that shape how people recover from a shock, one stands out in the research again and again. It isn't a technique, or a personality trait, or even the nature of the event. It's whether there are people around who help. This chapter is about the evidence, and about what kinds of help work.

In 2000, a team of British researchers set out to answer a simple question. Among all the things that might predict whether someone develops lasting post-traumatic stress after a traumatic event, which ones are the strongest? They combined the results of many studies, and the answer was clear.

Chris Brewin and his colleagues analysed seventy-seven studies. They found that the strongest predictors were factors that came after the event, such as a lack of social support and additional life stress. These were stronger than factors like the severity of the trauma itself, or a person's age or gender. What happened afterwards mattered as much as what happened.

show.where: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 2000
show.what: Meta-analysis of risk factors for posttraumatic stress disorder in trauma-exposed adults

segments.say: This is a hopeful finding, because what happens after an event is partly in our hands, and in the hands of the people around us. It means that supportive responses from friends, family and communities can change outcomes, and that withdrawal, blame or silence can make them worse.

Different kinds of support matter at different times. In the first days, practical help is often most valuable. Later, it's emotional support and companionship that people say they miss, when everyone else has gone back to their lives.

show.title: What counts as support
items: Informational: help finding services and answers

segments.say: The research has also looked at what happens when support is badly matched. One finding is that it's not enough for people to be around. They need to respond in a way that helps. Researchers call the opposite of this social constraint: the experience of feeling that you can't talk about what happened, because others seem uncomfortable, critical or unwilling to listen.

Stephen Lepore and his colleagues studied mothers who had lost a child. They found that those who felt that others were unwilling to hear about their loss reported more intrusive thoughts and more depression. Feeling that you can't talk, and the thoughts that you hold back, seem to compound each other.

show.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1996
show.what: Social constraints, intrusive thoughts, and depressive symptoms among bereaved mothers

segments.say: When people feel unable to talk, the thoughts don't go away. They go underground, where they tend to return in intrusive, unbidden forms. When people can talk and are heard, the thoughts can be put into words, shared, and gradually processed. This is one reason why the way we respond to someone else's pain matters so much.

The last one of these is hard for many of us. We want to fix it. But researchers find that people who have been through something terrible often want to tell the story many times, and each time they tell it, it changes a little. A good listener lets it happen without trying to finish it. It's one of the most generous things we can do.

show.title: Responses that help
items: Ask how they're doing today, not just in general
Let them tell it again, and again

segments.say: The research also suggests that it's not only whether we tell, but whom. A person who's safe, who has shown that they can listen without judging, is worth far more than a crowd of people who mean well but react badly. Many people find that a small number of trusted listeners is enough.

If you're the one who has been hurt, it can help to choose your listeners carefully. Think about who in your life has listened well before. It might be a friend, a relative, a counsellor or a support group of others who've been through something similar. Peer groups can be especially helpful, because the people there don't need an explanation.

Tedeschi and Calhoun, in their reviews of growth, emphasised that talking with others who've gone through a similar experience can be particularly valuable, because they can listen without being shocked, and can model what a path forward looks like. It's one reason why support groups, for bereavement and for many conditions, are so widely used.

show.what: Posttraumatic growth: conceptual foundations and empirical evidence

segments.say: Four terms from this chapter. Social support is the help that other people give. Social constraint is feeling unable to talk because others won't listen. Peer support is help from people who've been through the same thing. And a risk factor is something that raises the chance of a bad outcome. Picture this scene. A neighbour's husband dies in the spring. In the first week, the street fills with casseroles and cards. By the third month, the phone is quiet. One neighbour keeps knocking every Friday, and just sits for half an hour, rarely saying much. Years later the widow says that those Fridays were what carried her through. The research agrees with her. Support that is steady and unhurried, and that outlasts the first rush of sympathy, turns out to matter more than any single grand gesture.

show.title: Words to keep from this chapter

segments.say: Here are some ways to look after someone who's hurting, that follow from the research. Check in again after a month and after three months, when support has usually thinned out. Offer one specific thing, which is easier to accept than a general offer. Let them talk about the person or event, including the details, and don't change the subject to cheer them up. And ask what they need, then accept the answer, even when it's not what you'd have chosen. These are small acts. They are also among the best-supported things anyone can do.

show.title: Looking after a person who's hurting
items: Check in again at one month and three months
Offer one specific thing you can do
Let them talk about the person or event
Ask what they need, and accept the answer

segments.say: Two armchairs drawn close together, a blanket and a pot of tea. It's an ordinary scene, and the research says that it's among the most powerful things that exist. Someone to sit with, who doesn't need to say much, is a large part of what carries people through.

If you've been hurt, and you tend to cope on your own, the research offers a gentle nudge. People who have even one trusted person to talk to tend to do better. It may feel like a burden to ask. But most people want to help, and many are waiting to be asked. Letting someone in is often a gift to them as well.

So what did we learn? That lack of social support is among the strongest predictors of lasting distress. That feeling unable to talk can deepen it. That good support is practical, patient and long-lasting. And that choosing the right listeners makes a difference.

show.sub: What the people around us taught us

segments.say: Next, we'll look at a famous experiment that asked people to write about the worst things that had happened to them, for just fifteen minutes a day, and at what researchers later learned about whether it really works.
